lead: Paul tells the Colossians that their life “is hidden with Christ in God”. In the Gospel a woman tries to stay hidden in the crowd, touches the fringe of Jesus' clothes, and is healed; but Jesus will not let her slip away unnoticed, because he wants to give her more than a cure. The life hidden in God is not a life hidden from God. The key words are hidden and touch.

r.h: Your life is hidden with Christ in God
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). The letter names Paul as its author, writing from prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in his name, perhaps soon after his death; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way, the Church has always received it as inspired Scripture.

In chapter 2 the letter has said that in Baptism the Colossians were “buried with him” and “raised with him” (2:12). Today's verses are the hinge of the letter: they turn from teaching to daily life. What follows in 3:5–17 is very practical: put away anger and lies, put on compassion, forgive one another.
str: v. 1: you have been raised with Christ, so seek what is above.
v. 3: you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
v. 4: when Christ appears, you will appear with him in glory.
kw: A verb with the prefix “with”. The believer's rising is not a separate event from Christ's; it is a share in his. The same compound verb is used in 2:12.
Not a place in the sky, but the world where Christ now reigns “at the right hand of God”, the words of Psalm 110:1. To seek them is to let Christ's reign shape how we live now.
Hidden as treasure is hidden, kept safe, not lost. The new life is real already, but not yet visible to the world. It will be revealed when Christ appears (v. 4).
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
The “if” is not a doubt. It means “since”. Paul is reminding the baptized of what has already happened to them.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
A Christian's deepest identity cannot be seen on the surface. It is kept in God, where no failure or loss can reach it.
When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.
Some ancient manuscripts read “our life” instead of “your life”; the POC follows that reading. Either way, Christ is not only the giver of life. He is our life.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of the resurrection of the dead: united with Christ by Baptism, believers already share truly in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, but this life remains “hidden with Christ in God” until it is revealed (CCC 1002–1003). Seeking “the things above” does not mean neglecting the earth. The verses that follow fill everyday life, at home and at work, with the virtues of Christ. The Holy Qurbono itself joins earth to heaven: we lift up our hearts to where Christ is, and he comes down to us.

r.h: Daughter, your faith has made you well
set: Jesus has crossed back over the lake after healing the man among the tombs in the country of the Gerasenes (8:26–39). A crowd is waiting for him. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, begs him to come to his dying daughter, and on the way the woman's story is set inside his. Mark tells the same two stories in the same way (Mark 5:21–43). Both the girl and the woman's illness are marked by the number twelve.

The Law of Moses counted a woman with a long flow of blood as ritually unclean, and the same applied to what she touched (Leviticus 15:25–27). This concerned worship and the Temple, and the Gospel does not dwell on it. But it may help explain why she came quietly from behind.
str: vv. 40–42a: the crowd; Jairus' plea for his daughter.
vv. 42b–44: the woman touches the fringe and is healed at once.
vv. 45–46: “Who touched me?”; power has gone out.
v. 47: she comes trembling and tells everything.
v. 48: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
¶ The story of Jairus' daughter continues in 8:49–56.
kw: Probably the tassel that the Law told every Israelite man to wear on the corners of his cloak, to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus wore it as a faithful Jew. Matthew says that many were healed by touching it (Matthew 14:36).
The same word Luke uses of the Spirit's power (1:35; 24:49). Healing is not magic in the cloth. It is the power of God going out from the person of Jesus.
has made you well, has saved you
The Greek verb means both to heal and to save. The POC renders it “has saved you”. The woman came for a cure of the body and received salvation and peace.
vv: She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his clothes, and immediately her hemorrhage stopped.

Twelve years of failure end in a moment. Verse 43 adds that she had spent all she had on physicians; some important early manuscripts leave out those words, and Luke, whom tradition calls a physician (Colossians 4:14), is gentler with doctors than Mark is (Mark 5:26).
Someone touched me; for I noticed that power had gone out from me.
Many pressed on him; only one touched him in faith. St Augustine put it this way: the crowd presses, faith touches (in substance).
When the woman saw that she could not remain hidden, she came trembling;
Jesus calls her out not to shame her but to complete her healing in front of everyone, so that she is restored to the community.
Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.
In all three Gospels that tell this story, she is the only person Jesus addresses as “daughter”. She came as an outsider and leaves as one of the family.
ch: The Catechism recalls that the sick tried to touch Jesus, “for power came out from him and healed all of them” (Luke 6:19), and teaches that in the sacraments Christ continues to “touch” us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). The woman's faith was humble and bodily: she wanted to touch. That is the logic of the sacraments, where the grace of Christ reaches us through water, oil, bread and wine, and the hands of his priests.

study: Where am I hiding from the Lord, as the woman tried to hide in the crowd, and what would it mean to come forward to him?
Paul says my life is hidden with Christ in God. How does that change the way I see my failures and my successes?
